Name: Modder's Pie - A Complete Tutorial For Your First Mod
Author: SiTheGreat1
Description:
Hello there! I'm Si, the author of [url=https://www.nexusmods.com/stardewvalley/mods/12667]Morris Redeemed[/url], [url=https://www.nexusmods.com/stardewvalley/mods/18000]Adventurer Abigail[/url], and [url=https://www.nexusmods.com/stardewvalley/mods/21535]The Everything Bagel[/url] (among other mods), and today I'm going to walk you through making your very first mod! We'll go over the art, the code, the testing, and even how to set up a mod page here on Nexus.

This tutorial is meant to serve as an introduction to the world of Stardew Valley modmaking. I'm going to show you where and how to find resources so you can take what you learn from me and expand on it to come up with your own mods after you've made this one.

The mod files I created as part of this tutorial can be found on the Files page. You can download, look at, and even play with them at any time.

This tutorial assumes you've played with Stardew Valley mods before, and is written specifically for the 1.6 version of Stardew Valley. No C#, coding, or artistic knowledge is required. We will not be using AI, and I heavily discourage using it for any Stardew modding at all.

Today we're going to be adding a food item to the game: Modder's Pie! We'll also be adding the cooking recipe for the pie to Gus' shop at the Stardrop Saloon, so that the player can buy and cook the recipe.

Here's what you'll need:
- [b]A computer[/b]: most Stardew Valley modding requires the PC version of the game in order to work, and modmaking is no exception. Any OS will work; I'm using Windows, but making mods on Mac or Linux isn't any different.
- [b]A Nexus account[/b]: you'll need an account on here to make your mod page and upload your mod.
- [b]An official PC copy of Stardew Valley[/b]. You do not need to have a preexisting save for this tutorial (though it might help things go a bit quicker); instead, I'm going to show you a few handy tools for fast testing :)
- [b][url=https://www.nexusmods.com/stardewvalley/mods/2400]SMAPI[/url][/b]: this is the Stardew Modding API, which allows for the safe installation and running of Stardew Valley mods. If you've played with mods before, this would have been the first thing you downloaded.
- [url=https://www.nexusmods.com/stardewvalley/mods/1915]Content Patcher[/url] (version 2.9 or newer): this is a framework mod that provides an easy way for other mods to add features like items, maps, and even NPCs! We'll talk about frameworks a little more later.
- [url=https://www.nexusmods.com/stardewvalley/mods/4]CJB Cheats Menu[/url] and [url=https://www.nexusmods.com/stardewvalley/mods/93]CJB Item Spawner[/url]: these mods are super helpful for testing your own mods quickly.
- [url=https://github.com/Pathoschild/StardewXnbHack/releases]StardewXnbHack[/url]: despite the name, this is a legitimate tool for unpacking your copy of Stardew Valley so you can look at the games files easily. We'll go over how to download and use it a little bit later.
- [b]A text editor[/b]: which editor you use is your decision. Popular choices include VS Code and Notepad++, since they provide features like format-checking, but even something as simple as your computer's built-in Notepad can do. I'm using [url=https://code.visualstudio.com/download]VS Code[/url], but the process is the same for other text editors.
- [b]An art program[/b]: any program is fine as long as it has a pixel brush. Popular choices include Aseprite and GIMP. I'm using [url=https://www.getpaint.net/]paint.net[/url] because it's what I'm accustomed to, but the choice is yours. Depending on what you use, the buttons and layout may look a little different.

And that's it. Let's get started!


[size=5][b]Unpacking The Game
[/b][/size]
When making a mod, the first question you should ask yourself is 'what do I want to make?'. Luckily, I've already decided that for you :) we're making Modder's Pie today.

The second, and arguably more important, question you should ask yourself is 'how does the game already do that?'. The answer lies within the game files, so being able to look at them helps a lot.

When most games are made, their files are 'packed' to reduce the file size. Unfortunately, this makes them less readable by human eyes. You can 'see' this for yourself by going to your Stardew Valley game folder, and looking for a folder called 'Content'. It should be next to your Mods folder, where you place mods that you're playing with.

Open the Content folder, and inside it, open the Animals folder. You see all those XNB files? Those are the image files for the farm animals, but clicking on them doesn't show you that image. Your computer likely doesn't know how to open the file at all. Not very helpful, is it? Let's change that:

1. Close the Content folder.

2. Download StardewXnbHack by clicking its file name here: [url=https://github.com/Pathoschild/StardewXnbHack/releases]https://github.com/Pathoschild/StardewXnbHack/releases[/url]
Make sure you're downloading the version for your computer's OS, and not the source code!

2. Unzip the downloaded StardewXnbHack folder into your Stardew Valley game folder. Generally this is done by right-clicking the zipped folder and selecting 'Extract'.

3. Click the StardewXnbHack.exe file inside the unzipped folder. It may take a moment to work, but once it does, there should now be a new 'Content (Unpacked)' folder next to your Mods folder.

If you go into the Content (Unpacked) folder and then the Animals folder, you can now see the image files for the farm animals!


[b][size=5]Frameworks[/size][/b]

Most of the files in Content (Unpacked) are images (often called 'assets'), but there are maps and data files in there too. This tutorial won't go over map making or editing - that's a subject deserving of its own page - but we will talk about data files later when we look at game objects and shops.

The act of modding involves 'modifying' these files. Modifying files directly, such as by replacing XNB files, is difficult because it can cause errors in the game code, affect the player's save file, and break compatibility with other mods. So instead, we use frameworks like Content Patcher as a middleman to modify things safely.

Frameworks take the files we create for our mods and translate them into code that the game can read, while also catching bugs and ensuring multiple mods can work with each other. If you've ever played with a mod that required other mods to also be installed for it to work - like [url=https://www.nexusmods.com/stardewvalley/mods/17265]Unlockable Bundles[/url], [url=https://www.nexusmods.com/stardewvalley/mods/1348]SpaceCore[/url], or [url=https://www.nexusmods.com/stardewvalley/mods/3231]Farm Type Manager[/url] - then the mod you played with was likely dependent on those frameworks for some or all of its features.

There are many frameworks out there for various needs, and most of them don't require coding knowledge to use when making mods. Content Patcher is the most popular framework because of the sheer number of features it provides - you can make an entire NPC using that alone. You'll be able to start making an NPC using the skills you learn today, but that's a much larger project because of all the things required - walking sprites, portraits, dialogue, a schedule, and so forth. Let's keep it simple with a cooking recipe for now :)

Frameworks come with documentation on how to use them, usually linked on their mod page. We'll check out Content Patcher's documentation as we go through this tutorial.


[b][size=5]Starting The Mod[/size]
[/b]
Alright enough talk, let's make some mod files.

Create a folder inside your Mods folder. You can call it whatever you want; I'll be calling mine 'Modder's Pie'. All your mod's files will go inside this folder.

All mods have a minimum of two files:
- The manifest file that tells SMAPI the mod exists, called manifest.json
- The file containing the content of the mod. For Content Patcher mods, this is always called content.json

JSON is the file type used for most Stardew mod data files. To create a JSON file, simply create a text file and save it as .json

A few simple rules for JSON files:
- Every file should start and end with curly brackets. Start the file with { and end the file with }
- There should be a comma at the end of every line. There are some exceptions, but even if a comma isn't needed somewhere, it's still usually safe to add one anyway, so it's better to have one than not if you're unsure.
- Try to avoid having spaces in file and folder names. Underscores can be used instead.
- Some computer systems are case-sensitive, so make sure you match cases in all your file and folder names so you don't get bug reports about it.

Let's create the manifest.json file first. Manifest files all use a pretty similar format across Stardew mods.

1. Open a blank text file and place an open curly bracket in the first line like so: {

2. Copy and paste the following lines into the file (we'll talk about them more below):

[code]"Name": "Name of your mod here",
"Author": "Your username here",
"Description": "A quick description of your mod here.",
"Version": "1.0.0",
"UniqueID": "YourUsernameHere.YourModNameHere",
"UpdateKeys": [ "Nexus:" ],[/code]

3. Fill out the fields as described.

4. Because this is a Content Patcher mod, add these lines as well:

[code]"ContentPackFor": {
 "UniqueID": "Pathoschild.ContentPatcher",
 },[/code]
5. Place a closing curly bracket in the last line of the file like so: }

6. Save the file as manifest.json (make sure it's not saved as a .txt file!)


Let's go over some of these fields.

[b]Name[/b], [b]Author[/b], and [b]Description [/b]should be fairly self explanatory.

[b]Version[/b]: this shows what version of a mod you are using. Every time you update your mod, you should update the version number (both here and on Nexus, which we'll talk about later). In common convention:
- Increasing the first digit means you have made major changes to your mod, for example 1.0.0, 2.0.0, 3.0.0 etc
- Increasing the second digit means you have made minor changes or updates to your mod, for example 1.1.0, 1.2.0, 2.1.0 etc
- Increasing the third digit means you have fixed bugs or typos, for example 1.0.1, 1.3.4, 2.1.1 etc.

[b]UniqueID[/b]: this is your mod's unique internal name. Mods can have the same name as each other, but can still work together as long as their internal names are different, which is why it's important to include your username in there. This allows various mods to be compatible with each other.

[b]UpdateKeys[/b]: This will be your Nexus ID when you make your mod page, and allows SMAPI to check for updates when running. We'll talk more about that later.

[b]ContentPackFor[/b]: this is specific to Content Patcher, which means it's time to take a look at Content Patcher's documentation: [url=https://github.com/Pathoschild/StardewMods/blob/stable/ContentPatcher/docs/author-guide.md]https://github.com/Pathoschild/StardewMods/blob/develop/ContentPatcher/docs/author-guide.md[/url]
The documentation covers everything Content Patcher can do, and has a very helpful Table Of Contents at the top. Many of the sections also link to other documentation pages - useful when you're digging into something specific. For now, click on 'Get Started', which will scroll you down to the Create A Content Pack section showing you exactly what we just went over, including the 'ContentPackFor' line we just added to the manifest.json.

Now that you've seen it, let's leave the Content Patcher documentation alone for a while. Your manifest.json file should look something like this, personalized to you:

[code]{
"Name": "Modder's Pie",
"Author": "SiTheGreat1",
"Description": "A hearty slice of pie for aspiring modmakers!",
"Version": "1.0.0",
"UniqueID": "SiTheGreat1.ModdersPie",
"UpdateKeys": [ "Nexus:" ],
"ContentPackFor": {
  "UniqueID": "Pathoschild.ContentPatcher",
},
}[/code]

Great! Now that we have our manifest.json ready, let's make our content.json file.

1. Open a blank text file and place an open curly bracket in the first line like so: {

2. Add this line to the top of the file under the curly bracket:
[code]"Format": "2.9.0",[/code]This line tells Content Patcher which version of itself to use when interpreting your mod. Newer versions of Content Patcher may have new features, but may also require new formatting. For this tutorial, we'll use version 2.9.0 as it's the newest version at the time this tutorial is being written.
You don't have to update this number every time Content Patcher updates unless you are updating your own mod to make use of a new feature being introduced in Content Patcher.

3. Add this line under the Format line:
[code]"Changes": [[/code]The Changes section is where all the actual mod changes (often called 'patches') that you'll be making will go.

4. Add a closing square bracket under the Changes line like so: ]
This will mark the end of the Changes section.

5. Place a closing curly bracket in the last line of the file like so: }

6. Save the file as content.json (make sure it's not saved as a .txt file!)

Your content.json file should look like this:

[code]{

"Format": "2.9.0",

"Changes": [

]

}[/code]

And you now have the base foundation used by the vast majority of Stardew Valley mods! Time to populate it with your own mod :)


[b][size=5]The Item Sprite[/size]
[/b]
We are going to be creating a pie item, which involves the following steps:
1. Create the pie art
2. Load the art into the game
3. Create the pie object and tell it to use that art
4. Test the object
5. Create the recipe for the pie
6. Add the recipe to the saloon shop
7. Test the recipe
8. Make the mod page

We're going to take a break from JSON files to do a little art. Start by opening up your art program of choice; as previously mentioned, I am using paint.net.

The biggest rule about art in Stardew modding is size; the height and width of sprites need to fall within specific dimensions for most things. NPCs, for example, must be 16 pixels wide and 32 pixels tall, and character portraits are 64 by 64 pixels. There are frameworks to get around size requirements, but we're not using them here, so we're restricted to the standard sizes.

Typical Stardew objects must fit within a 16 by 16 pixel square. There are exceptions for things like furniture and machines, but food isn't among them.

Let's start by resizing our canvas to 16 by 16 pixels. You can keep it bigger for now so you have space to work and then resize it later, if you prefer.

To do this in paint.net, I go to Image > Canvas Size and set the Width and Height, then click OK. If the file started with a white background, then I also get rid of it by selecting it with the magic wand tool and pressing delete, that so I'm left with a transparent background.

[img]https://staticdelivery.nexusmods.com/mods/1303/images/43811/43811-1773814366-168590999.png[/img]

There's options that make spriting easier like using layers and setting background pixel size that you can play around with, but as far as this tutorial goes I'm keeping it simple, with everything on one layer.

Now's the part where you can do whatever the heck you want. As long as it's within the bounds of 16 by 16 pixels, you can go absolutely wild in designing your pie. Heck, it doesn't even need to look like a pie. Just grab the pencil tool and pixel it up to your heart's content.

Behold! My masterpiece.
[img]https://staticdelivery.nexusmods.com/mods/1303/images/43811/43811-1773814372-808971804.png[/img]

If you'd like to go for something in Stardew Valley's art style, you can check out the actual game's art in your freshly unpacked Content (Unpacked) folder. Most objects (including food) can be found in the Maps folder in a file called springobjects.png

(If you're wondering why the objects file is in the maps folder... yeah, so is every other Stardew modder lol)

There's also resources out there on pixel spriting, including Stardew's specific style. I'm partial to this one in particular: [url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220204164234/https://sundrop.kvdk.net/files/SundropArtGuide.pdf]https://web.archive.org/web/20220204164234/https://sundrop.kvdk.net/files/SundropArtGuide.pdf[/url]

Once you've got a sprite you're happy with, save it as a .png file in your mod's folder. I've named mine pie.png

Your mod folder should now look like this:

[img]https://staticdelivery.nexusmods.com/mods/1303/images/43811/43811-1773814396-1284718712.png[/img]

Now that we have art, let's get back to writing mod patches.


[b][size=5]Loading Art[/size]
[/b]
Open your content.json file. You're going to write your first patch, which is a collection of lines telling Content Patcher what to do.

Each patch has an Action field. This tells Content Patcher what type of action it is. Let's return to the Content Patcher documentation: [url=https://github.com/Pathoschild/StardewMods/blob/stable/ContentPatcher/docs/author-guide.md]https://github.com/Pathoschild/StardewMods/blob/develop/ContentPatcher/docs/author-guide.md[/url]

In the Table Of Contents, click on Actions under Features. Here, you can see what each type of Action does. Some actions load data or images (assets), some edit existing data, and some tell it to include data from other sources. Since we're loading an image that doesn't exist in the game yet (the pie art), we'll be using a Load Action.

All patches start and end with curly brackets: {}
Under the Changes line in your content.json, place an open curly bracket, and then on the next line, write the Load Action line like so:

[code]"Changes": [
{
  "Action": "Load",
},
][/code]

Make sure each side of the line is enclosed in quotation marks, and end each line with a comma.

You'll notice these lines have some space between the start of the line and the first character. This is called 'indentation', and you can do it by pressing the Tab key on your keyboard. Indenting lines is useful for keeping track of bracket pairs so you don't leave any bracketed sections open by accident.

Let's also add a comment. This is a line that the game doesn't read; it's there to help people like yourself know what the line is for. This helps a lot when you look at a patch you made two years ago at 3am because someone's found a bug and now they won't play the game until you fix it because they desperately want pie.

Comments in JSON files start with two slashes like so: //

You should always add comments with notes explaining what you're doing, and even why. Trust me, you'll be glad you did later.

You can also comment patches to temporarily disable them (or parts of them) while testing!

[code]"Changes": [

// Patch to load pie art
{
  "Action": "Load", // This is a load action
},
][/code]

Next, you're going to tell Content Patcher where to find the image using the FromFile field. Since the image is in your main folder, this will just be the image name and file extension, for example "pie.png". If you organized your art in a separate subfolder within your mod folder, then this would include the path to that folder, for example "SubFolderName/pie.png".

Add the FromFile field to your patch:

[code]    // Patch to load pie art
{
  "Action": "Load",
  "FromFile": "pie.png",
},[/code]
Finally, add the Target field to your patch. This tells Content Patcher where to store the art inside the game. The standard target for modded items is "Mods/{{ModId}}/YourObjectHere".

"{{ModId}}" is your mod's UniqueID, that you created in the manifest.json file. You do not have to write your actual UniqueID in the Target field. The double curly brackets around word 'ModId' here automatically format this field into your UniqueID for you, so you don't have to keep rewriting it.

Using your UniqueID ensures your mod's objects are unique compared to other mods. This means that if two people both publish their own versions of Modder's Pie using the exact same formatting and file names, they will be compatible with each other, because of the uniqueness preserved by the UniqueID. That's why it's important to use "{{ModId}}" for everything you add to the game - objects, NPCs, cutscenes, etc.

Now, let's add the Target field:

[code]    // Patch to load pie art
{
  "Action": "Load",
  "FromFile": "pie.png",
  "Target": "Mods/{{ModId}}/ModdersPie",
},[/code]

Your art is now loaded into the game!


[b][size=5]Creating Objects[/size]
[/b]
You may now be asking 'so where is it?'. Great question!

Even though the game now knows where to find the art, it doesn't know what to do with it yet. We now need to create an object, and then tell the game that the art is for that object.

Stardew Valley, on its own, contains hundreds of objects - crops, fish, furniture, etc. Knowing that, we can assume that there must be a data file where those objects are created. So let's find it!

Go to your Content (Unpacked) folder and open the Data folder inside it. This is where most of Stardew's data files are located. Some (especially NPC schedules and dialogue) are found in other folders in the Content (Unpacked) folder; I leave it as an exercise to you, dear reader, to find them :)

Scroll through the Data folder; eventually you'll find the Objects.json file. Open it up, and you'll find entries defining almost every standard object in the game (special ones like shirts and fish have their own, similar, files).

These entries provide a guide for what the game is looking for when you patch something into it, so knowing where they are is very helpful. That having been said, I doubt you want to run through all of the entries trying to figure out what's necessary for your pie, so let's look at another popular resource: the Modding Wiki.

[url=https://stardewvalleywiki.com/Modding:Index]https://stardewvalleywiki.com/Modding:Index[/url]

Now, the Content Patcher documentation tells you how to use Content Patcher, but it doesn't tell you the definitions of every type of data in the game. Whatever you're looking to make, the Modding Wiki probably has a page on it. And if it doesn't, well, now you know how to check the Content (Unpacked) folder too!

But for this pie, we'll use the Wiki. Since it's an object, scroll down the Wiki Index page until you find Item Data, and then click on Objects.

You're going to be greeted with a page with lots of info on it. Let's learn how to focus on just the info you need for your next patch.

Since you now know (from your adventures in the Content (Unpacked) folder) that an Objects file already exists, you don't need to Load a new Objects file. Instead, we'll be using the EditData Action to edit the existing Objects file. You can read more about EditData in the Content Patcher documentation.

So, underneath your previous patch, let's start a new one

[code]    // Patch to load pie art
{
  "Action": "Load",
  "FromFile": "pie.png",
  "Target": "Mods/{{ModId}}/ModdersPie",
},
// Patch to create pie object
{
  "Action": "EditData",
},[/code]

We will be targeting Data/Objects, since that is where the current game Objects file is located. Do not include the file extension on this line; Content Patcher handles that part.

[code]    // Patch to create pie object
{
  "Action": "EditData",
  "Target": "Data/Objects",
},[/code]
Each item in Data/Objects is an entry. Since we are adding a new entry, we will have an Entries field in our patch, and we will define our object inside it.

[code]    // Patch to create pie object
{
  "Action": "EditData",
  "Target": "Data/Objects",
  "Entries": {
  },
},[/code]
You can have multiple entries within the Entries field. Today, we're only going to have one: Modder's Pie.

Let's start referencing the Modding Wiki Objects page as we define the object.

On the Wiki page, the Data Format says you need a Key and a Value. The Key is the object's internal name. The Value is the rest of the object's fields.

Sometimes the object's name needs to be 'qualified', which means it needs to have a signifier attached to its name telling the game what it is. This signifier looks like (O) for objects, (S) for shirts, (W) for weapons and so on. For example, '(O)pie' is a qualified name, 'pie' is unqualified.

Definitions in the Wiki will tell you if they require a a qualified object name that includes one of these signifiers, so watch out for that.

You may also notice some old game items have numbers instead of names. This was part of the old system (1.5 and older); all newer item types have wordy names like 'ThingyMcThingFace' and 'pleasework2_final'. Just remember to include "{{ModId}}" at the beginning of your modded item's internal names so they preserve their uniqueness.

I'll be calling my pie "{{ModId}}_ModdersPie". You are free to do the same, or come up with your own name, as long as it still starts with "{{ModId}}_". Let's add the Key to the patch:

[code]    // Patch to create pie object
{
  "Action": "EditData",
  "Target": "Data/Objects",
  "Entries": {
"{{ModId}}_ModdersPie": {
},
  },
},[/code]

If you wanted to add multiple pies, you'd simply add the next Key-Value pair under the last one (with a different name), like this:

[code]    // Patch to create pie objects
{
  "Action": "EditData",
  "Target": "Data/Objects",
  "Entries": {
// Pie 1
"{{ModId}}_ModdersPie": {
},
// Pie 2
"{{ModId}}_ModdersPie2": {
},
  },
},[/code]

But we're only adding one today, so let's keep going.

Up next are the object definition fields. These are the tables in the Data Format section of the Objects Wiki. Some fields are required, others are optional. If a field is optional, it might have a value that it defaults to if not specified, so read the description of each field carefully in case you don't want it to do that.

Let's start with the Basic Info table:

[code]    // Patch to create pie objects
{
  "Action": "EditData",
  "Target": "Data/Objects",
  "Entries": {
"{{ModId}}_ModdersPie": {
"Name": "{{ModId}}_ModdersPie", // This is your object's internal name. Yes, it's the same as the Key.
"DisplayName": "Modder's Pie", // The name you want the player to see when they select the object in-game.
"Description": "A healthy slice of Modder's Pie, just for you!", // The pop-up describing the object when you hover over it in game.
"Type": "Cooking", // Foods are a 'Cooking' type. There's a list of types in the Type field description in the Basic Info table.
"Category": -7, // The item's category. There's a link to category numbers in the table. We want the Cooking category, which is -7.
"Price": 150, // This field is optional. Set it to whatever you like!
},
  },
},[/code]

As you can see, we're starting to rely on the Wiki to explain terms to you rather than dear ol' Si. This is the part where you get to start spreading your wings, because now you know where to find information :D

Let's use the Appearance table to add the art you loaded to the object:

[code]    // Patch to create pie objects
{
  "Action": "EditData",
  "Target": "Data/Objects",
  "Entries": {
"{{ModId}}_ModdersPie": {
"Name": "{{ModId}}_ModdersPie",
"DisplayName": "Modder's Pie",
"Description": "A healthy slice of Modder's Pie, just for you!",
"Type": "Cooking",
"Category": -7,
"Price": 150,
"Texture": "Mods/{{ModId}}/ModdersPie", // This is where you tell the object what art to use!
"SpriteIndex": 0, // You can have multiple objects in one image. If you do, you can tell this object which one to use here. The first 16 by 16 pixel square in the image is always 0, so use that if it's the only square.
},
  },
},[/code]

Finally, let's set the object's Edibility. This defines how much health and energy the player gains (or loses) when eating the pie.

On the Wiki, right after the Appearance table should be the Edibility table. It's got a couple of fields in it: Edibility, IsDrink, and Buffs. Since all of them are optional, we're just going to add the Edibility field within the table to our pie for now, as it's the only one required to make a food able to be eaten.

As you can see from the field description, it's got some calculation involved. You can either come up with some fun values, OR you can use your new Content (Unpacked) adventuring skills to go explore the game's Objects.json file and find other Stardew food items to pick values from.

I won't include what I put for Edibility here. You can look at other food items in the game's Objects.json file to see what the format of the Edibility line should look like if you're having trouble setting it up; it should be similar to how you've set up lines for other fields so far.

That's everything for creating a basic object. If you'd like to play around with yours some more, feel free to experiment with the other fields in the Objects Wiki tables!


[b][size=5]Testing Objects[/size]
[/b]
Congratulations, you've officially made a mod! We're not done yet, but let's pause and make sure we're on the right track.

First, take at least a 20 minute break. Use the bathroom, drink some water, and gaze longingly out the window for as long as you can. Please. Do it for me <3

Now that we're rested and refreshed, let's find out if your mod actually works!

Save your files, make sure they're in your Mods folder, and open Stardew Valley using SMAPI the way you usually do when playing mods.

Something you're going to get used to as a modmaker is keeping an eye on the SMAPI window (the window with lots of text that opens alongside Stardew) whenever you open the game. That's good practice, so you can catch any errors or red text early.

You might notice the SMAPI window telling you that Modder's Pie 'has no update keys'. That's alright - you'll add an update key to the manifest.json when you create your Nexus mod page. For now, it's safe to ignore that message.

You can either open an existing save or start a new one. In this case I recommend opening an existing save if you have one; you won't be saving/sleeping or making any changes to it, as you'll only be in that save for a couple minutes in-game.

Once you've got your farmer in front of you, go to the SMAPI window and type the following:

[code]debug item UniqueID_ModdersPie[/code]
Replace UniqueID with your Unique ID, which should be YourUsernameHere.YourModNameHere

But Si, you say, shouldn't it be "{{ModId}}_ModdersPie"?

Yes! BUT...

Your UniqueID is internal to your own mod. Content Patcher knows what "{{ModId}}" means, but SMAPI does not. It's got loads of other mods using "{{ModId}}", so it can't tell which mod you're targeting. You have to tell it to target your own mod by typing out your UniqueID.

For example, I type this into SMAPI:

[code]debug item SiTheGreat1.ModdersPie_ModdersPie[/code]
Now you do similar, replacing my username with yours (and any other differences your object's internal name may have).

What does this do? If you switch back to the game, and all went well, you should now see your pie in your farmer's inventory! Take a bite out of it to make sure you can eat it.

[img]https://staticdelivery.nexusmods.com/mods/1303/images/43811/43811-1773814429-84521599.png[/img]

(If it didn't go well, please let me know so we can figure out why!)

What you just used was a Console Command - commands that can be entered into SMAPI to cause things to happen. They feel cheaty in regular gameplay, but are an essential part of modmaking if you don't want to start a new save from scratch every time you test a new mod. In fact, the Modding Wiki has a whole page on them! Search for the Console Commands page under Special Topics > Game in the Modding Wiki Index to find the full list of commands. Remember to include 'debug' before every command.

Let's do one more command in SMAPI before closing Stardew:

[code]patch export Data/Objects[/code]
Unlike the above Console Commands, this one is a Content Patcher special. It makes a copy of Data/Objects that includes all modded items, and it puts that copy in a new folder it makes in the Stardew Valley folder called 'patch export'. If you open it, you can see everything that is currently part of Data/Objects, both regular and modded. Search for your username in there, and you'll find your pie! This is a helpful way to troubleshoot issues, since you can see what info the game is receiving from your patch.

Content Patcher commands like patch export can be found in the Content Patcher documentation 'Troubleshoot' section in the Table Of Contents. We'll look at another Content Patcher command later when we do the shop patch.


[b][size=5]Creating The Recipe[/size]
[/b]
Alright, next up is the cooking recipe for the pie! Close your game and hop over to the Recipes page in the Modding Wiki Index.

This Wiki page has both cooking and crafting recipes because they have similar formats. And when it comes to those formats, they're not as elegant as the object patch was. This is because they still use a legacy format from 1.5 and previous versions of the game. Eventually (hopefully) they'll be upgraded to use the standard data format most other data entries now use, but in the mean time, this is what we have to work with :')

As with the object entry, you can take a look at Data/CookingRecipes to see what standard recipes look like. But in this case, it might be more helpful to open up Data/Objects again instead, because that's where you'll be selecting ingredients for your pie.

This is where knowledge of the game comes into play. What would you like your pie to be made of? It can be whatever you want. Once you've come up with a list of ingredients, search Data/Objects for those ingredients.

Back when we started creating the pie object, I mentioned that some older game objects have numbers instead of names. You'll see this in Data/Objects. For example, the numerical ID of Daffodil is 18. Newer objects use actual names. For example, Mystery Boxes are internally called 'MysteryBox' instead of a number.

Gather all the internal names of the ingredients you want to cook your pie. As I proved in [url=https://www.nexusmods.com/stardewvalley/mods/21535]The Everything Bagel[/url], you can have as many as you want!

(While you do that, I'd like to take a brief moment to humbly apologize to the author of the fantastic mod [url=https://www.nexusmods.com/stardewvalley/mods/11115]Better Crafting[/url], which required an update to properly display the "absurd number of ingredients" my mod introduced. Sorry Khloe!)

Here's a list of ingredients I'll be using in my pie:
2 Wheat Flour (ID 246)
1 Chocolate Cake (220)
2 Eggs (any type) (-5)
1 Book Of Stars (PurpleBook)
3 Stone (390)

(No, they don't all have to be actual food.)

Notice that I used -5 for eggs; this refers to the item category section we saw when making our object patch. There are categories like this specifically for things like eggs, milk, fish etc. This allows the player to use any eggs they have for the recipe rather than specifying a single type.

Alright, let's start our next patch! Today we will be EditData-ing Data/CookingRecipes.

[code]    // Add cooking recipe
{
  "Action": "EditData",
  "Target": "Data/CookingRecipes",
  "Entries": {
  },
},[/code]

The thing about these older data models is that they're separated by slashes. The Wiki table specifying the values makes a little more sense when you look at Data/CookingRecipes. Let's make the full recipe entry before we place it inside the Entries field so it's easier to see what we're doing. We'll go step by step:

[code]"{{ModId}}_ModdersPie": "", // The entry's name can be the same as the object name for the pie for simplicity.

"{{ModId}}_ModdersPie": "246 2 220 1 -5 2 PurpleBook 1 390 3", // For each ingredient, we put the ingredient's ID first and the amount of that ingredient second.

"{{ModId}}_ModdersPie": "246 2 220 1 -5 2 PurpleBook 1 390 3/25 5", // The field following the slash is unused. I use the placeholder numbers 25 5 from the Wiki, and you can too.

"{{ModId}}_ModdersPie": "246 2 220 1 -5 2 PurpleBook 1 390 3/25 5/{{ModId}}_ModdersPie", // The next field is the output item made when the player cooks the recipe. In other words, this should be your pie.

"{{ModId}}_ModdersPie": "246 2 220 1 -5 2 PurpleBook 1 390 3/25 5/{{ModId}}_ModdersPie/none", // Next up is the unlock condition for the recipe. Since we'll be selling this recipe at the Stardrop Saloon, use 'none' here.

"{{ModId}}_ModdersPie": "246 2 220 1 -5 2 PurpleBook 1 390 3/25 5/{{ModId}}_ModdersPie/none/Modder's Pie", // And finally, the display name of the pie.[/code]

Great, now that we have our entry, let's add it to the patch:

[code]    // Add cooking recipe
{
  "Action": "EditData",
  "Target": "Data/CookingRecipes",
  "Entries": {
"{{ModId}}_ModdersPie": "246 2 220 1 -5 2 PurpleBook 1 390 3/25 5/{{ModId}}_ModdersPie/none/Modder's Pie",
  },
},[/code]


[b][size=5]Adding The Recipe To The Shop[/size]
[/b]
Finally, the last part of our mod: letting the player purchase a recipe from the shop. More specifically, from Gus at the Stardrop Saloon.

Good news, you've already got most of the skills you need for this! So I'm going to introduce three more, just to really get you going.

[b]First: Include Actions.
[/b]
Remember how, in the Content Patcher documentation, there were multiple types of Actions? We've seen two so far: Load and EditData. Now we're going to talk about Include.

The Include Action allows you to split your patches up into multiple files. This helps a lot wth organizing, and it keeps your content.json from turning into a mess of 1000+ lines where you struggle to find anything. You always have to have a core content.json, but you can have more files named different things as well. We'll practice this by using Include for our shop patch.

[b]Next: TargetFields.
[/b]
TargetFields allows you to edit things inside of existing entries. For example, if you wanted to change the price of your pie using a separate patch, you would target the Price field inside the "{{ModId}}_ModdersPie" object entry. Since shops are entries in the Data/Shops file, and we need to edit one of those entries specifically (the Saloon shop), we'll be using this to add our recipe to that shop.

[b]Finally: When Conditions.
[/b]
When conditions allow you to specify things that have to happen before your patch is applied. We'll use this to make sure your recipe doesn't show up at the Saloon until after the player has upgraded their farmhouse.

Alright, let's get started!

Inside your mod folder, create a new JSON file. In case you forgot, that means making a text file, and saving it as a .json file instead of a .txt file.

You can name this file whatever you want. I'm going to call mine shop.json for simplicity.

Inside shop.json (or whatever you called yours), add opening and closing curly brackets the same way we did to the other two files, like so:

[code]{

}[/code]

And between those brackets, add a Changes line, just like we did with content.json.

[code]{
"Changes": [

]
}[/code]

The shop.json file should now look similar to what your content.json file looked like before we started adding patches to it, EXCEPT for one thing: shops.json should NOT have a Format line. That line stays purely within the content.json file.

Now let's set up the shop patch in shop.json:

[code]{
"Changes": [

  // Add recipe to Saloon shop
  {
"Action": "EditData",
"Target": "Data/Shops",
  },

]
}[/code]

Open up Data/Shops and have a look at what we're working with. You'll see that each shop entry starts with a Key (for example, the first shop's Key is AdventureGuildRecovery), followed by the various fields applicable to it. Everything from shop owners, to opening times, to items that the player can sell to it. It looks like a lot, but don't worry - it's no more complex than Data/Objects, there's just a lot more lines in each entry than what we're used to.

The Modding Wiki Shops page breaks it all down, but right now we're focused on the Items field. That's the field that contains everything the shop sells, so that's what we're going to be modifying for the Saloon shop using TargetField.

First, let's find the Saloon shop's Key in Data/Shops. Generally, you can find shops by searching either the building's name or the name of one of the shop's owners. It's not always immediately clear; for example, Pierre's shop is called SeedShop, and searching Pierre will give you multiple entries because of all the festival shops he runs.

Luckily for us, the Saloon shop is simply called Saloon. Thank goodness for reasonable people like Gus.

Now, let's set up the TargetField line. If you open the Content Patcher documentation and return to the Actions section, under EditData you'll see a link to more detailed documentation about EditData. Go to that page, and then search its Table Of Contents for the Target Field section. This section includes a table and some examples to show you how to use the command.

In our case, the target ID is the Saloon, and the target field name is Items, since we're adding a new entry to the Items field. We aren't editing a preexisting item, so we don't need the additional target list name or list index.
[code]
// Add recipe to Saloon shop
{
  "Action": "EditData",
  "Target": "Data/Shops",
  "TargetField": [ "Saloon", "Items" ],
},[/code]

Once we have our TargetField, we can move on to Entries, similar to how we did our object entry.

 
[code]  // Add recipe to Saloon shop
{
  "Action": "EditData",
  "Target": "Data/Shops",
  "TargetField": [ "Saloon", "Items" ],
  "Entries": {
"{{ModId}}_ModdersPie": {
},
  },
},[/code]

Now, the Items section of the Shops Wiki has a lot of fields, but it also draws from Item Spawn Fields, which are 'common fields' shared by various entries. Because of this, they have their own section of the Wiki, and are linked in the Items section table of the Shop Wiki. This means you should include any required Item Spawn Fields.

[code]// Add recipe to Saloon shop
{
  "Action": "EditData",
  "Target": "Data/Shops",
  "TargetField": [ "Saloon", "Items" ],
  "Entries": {
"{{ModId}}_ModdersPie": {
"Id": "{{ModId}}_ModdersPie",
"ItemId": "{{ModId}}_ModdersPie",
},
  },
},[/code]

You'll see mentions of Item Queries around the Item Spawn Fields section. Those are powerful methods of item selection using things like categories and randomization. We won't cover them here, but they're worth looking into to give your mods an extra kick :)

There's one more field we'll look at in Item Spawn Fields before returning to the Shops Wiki: the IsRecipe field. Notice how we used the item ID of the pie itself in the above shop patch. If we don't specify that it has to be a recipe, then the game will only add the pie itself to the Saloon shop. Let's add this field:

[code]    // Add recipe to Saloon shop
{
  "Action": "EditData",
  "Target": "Data/Shops",
  "TargetField": [ "Saloon", "Items" ],
  "Entries": {
"{{ModId}}_ModdersPie": {
"Id": "{{ModId}}_ModdersPie",
"ItemId": "{{ModId}}_ModdersPie",
"IsRecipe": true,
},
  },
},[/code]

Finally, let's go back to the Shops Wiki and add any other fields we'd like. I'll add Price because I want the cost of the recipe to be more than the cost of a single pie, but the choice is yours.

[code]    // Add recipe to Saloon shop
{
  "Action": "EditData",
  "Target": "Data/Shops",
  "TargetField": [ "Saloon", "Items" ],
  "Entries": {
"{{ModId}}_ModdersPie": {
"Id": "{{ModId}}_ModdersPie",
"ItemId": "{{ModId}}_ModdersPie",
"IsRecipe": true,
"Price": "1000",
},
  },
},[/code]

And that's our shop.json file done! Let's close it and return to our content.json file.

We'll now add the Include Action patch to tell the game that shop.json is part of the mod. Add this Action under your previous patches:

[code]    // Patch to include shop.json
{
  "Action": "Include",
  "FromFile": "shop.json",
},[/code]

Now, a cooking recipe is useless to the player unless they have a way to cook it. Yes, they could use a cookout kit, but such a magnificent pie deserves nothing less than a decent kitchen.

With that in mind, we're going to place a When condition on the Include patch so that the recipe only gets added to the Saloon shop after the player has upgraded their house.

You can find information on When conditions in the Content Patcher documentation under Tokens & Conditions; there's a link at the bottom of the section leading to further documentation.

In that further documentation, you're going to see a lot of mentions of Tokens. Tokens are like entries in the When field; we use them to set conditions. For example, the Season token can be used to set 'must be Summer' as a When condition.

If you search 'farmhouse' on that page, you'll find the FarmhouseUpgrade token. That's what we'll use inside our Include patch. Let's start by setting up the When field:

[code]    // Patch to include shop.json
{
  "Action": "Include",
  "FromFile": "shop.json",
  "When": {

  },
},[/code]

Inside the When field, we'll use the Token as the Key:

[code]    // Patch to include shop.json
{
  "Action": "Include",
  "FromFile": "shop.json",
  "When": {
"FarmhouseUpgrade": "", // We'll fill out the value next.
  },
},[/code]

A lot of tokens are 'Boolean', which means their value is either true or false. The IsRecipe field we saw earlier in the shop patch is an example of a Boolean value.

As seen in the Tokens table, however, FarmhouseUpgrade has its own values, which are numbers. We are targeting FarmhouseUpgrade value 1, which is true when the kitchen is added to the farmhouse.

That means the condition should be this, right?

[code]"FarmhouseUpgrade": "1",[/code]
Not necessarily. This is where you start to use that smart brain that got you this far :)

There's two things to consider here.

[b]First[/b]: if the When condition is only true when FarmhouseUpgrade is at 1, then it will become false when the player upgrades to the next level, FarmhouseUpgrade 2. this means if the player forgets to buy the recipe before upgrading again, they're out of luck for getting it back.

There's a couple different ways of fixing this. We'll keep it simple for now by using the 'Contains' argument. Details about 'Contains' can be found in the Input Arguments section of the Tokens page in the Content Patcher documentation.

[code]"FarmhouseUpgrade |contains=1, 2, 3": true,[/code]
This will allow the condition to be true at any of those upgrade levels.

[b]Second[/b]: as a modmaker, a question you're going to get asked a lot is whether your mod is compatible with multiplayer. In a multiplayer save, players can upgrade their farmhouses at different times, so you should consider that in your conditions.

At the bottom of the Tokens page, there's a section called 'Target Player'. You can use this to specify which player the condition should consider when applying the patch. We're going to use 'anyPlayer' so that the patch applies once any player has upgraded their house:

[code]"FarmhouseUpgrade:anyPlayer |contains=1, 2, 3": true,[/code]
Now let's update the When condition:

[code]    // Patch to include shop.json
{
  "Action": "Include",
  "FromFile": "shop.json",
  "When": {
"FarmhouseUpgrade:anyPlayer |contains=1, 2, 3": true,
  },
},[/code]

Hooray! Your mod is now complete. Now it's time to test it.


[b][size=5]Testing Your Mod[/size]
[/b]
You can use Console Commands to set everything up if you want to, but let's simplify things instead this time. We're going to use a pair of handy mods called the [url=https://www.nexusmods.com/stardewvalley/mods/4]CJB Cheats Menu[/url] and the [url=https://www.nexusmods.com/stardewvalley/mods/93]CJB Item Spawner[/url].

Similar to Console Commands, the CJB mods are pretty, well, cheaty in regular gameplay, but they're practically essential for mod testing. They basically give you an in-game interface for most of those Console Commands. Install both of them to your Mods folder before opening Stardew using SMAPI again.

We're going to use a fresh save this time. Type some gibberish in the name and favorite thing fields, use the randomizer, and select Skip Intro for a quick start to your farm. Sleep a day immediately to lock the test save in.

Quick tip: you can use this opportunity to create a dedicated test save if you'd like. It's basically a save where you mess things up on purpose while you learn modding. It's fun!

Let's set a few cheats up to start with. Press the hotkey for CJB Cheats ('p' if you didn't change it in the config) to open that menu. Go ahead and give yourself the Key To The Town in the Advanced tab, and enable Freeze Time Everywhere in the Time tab. Then press the hotkey for CJB Items ('i' if you didn't change it), search for 'chest', and give yourself a big ol' chest to dump stuff into.

Other options I've found helpful in my test save: increase move speed and inventory size, spawn iridium tools, instant build (won't work for the farmhouse), and give gifts anytime (for NPC testing). Don't go all out on the rest - you may want to avoid triggering some conditions yet so you can use them to test other mods in the future.

Sleep another night to save all the stuff you just did, and let's get to testing!

Use the Time tab to shift time to later in the day (some time when Gus will be tending the Saloon) and then head there. Your goal right now is to confirm that your recipe isn't showing up yet, since your house hasn't been upgraded.

Once Gus is at the bar, open the shop menu and check that the Modder's Pie recipe is NOT for sale. If it's not for sale, then that's good so far!

If you'd like to be extra sure, you can patch export Data/Shops (like we did with Data/Objects earlier) and check if Modder's Pie is in the file. It shouldn't be!

Once you've confirmed it's not for sale yet, it's time to satisfy your When condition by upgrading your house. Sleep a day to lock in the current state of the game, then set the time to one when Robin will be tending her shop. If it's Tuesday in game then you might have to change the day as well.

Once you've got her shop, use CJB to give yourself enough cash and wood to buy the house upgrade. You'll have to sleep 3 days for the upgrade to be finished.

Once it's done, change the time so Gus will head to the bar again and go check the Saloon shop. The recipe should be there now! Go ahead, buy it, and head home to cook it in your fancy new kitchen :)

[img]https://staticdelivery.nexusmods.com/mods/1303/images/43811/43811-1773814465-1341914839.png[/img]

Use CJB Items to spawn in your chosen ingredients, head to the stove, and cook yourself a hearty helping of Modder's pie!

[img]https://staticdelivery.nexusmods.com/mods/1303/images/43811/43811-1773814475-1714791863.png[/img]

You've now successfully tested your mod. Let's do one more thing before you close your game.

With the game still open, open your content.json file and go to your object patch. Change the description field of the pie. For example, I changed mine from "A healthy slice of Modder's Pie, just for you!", to "Dang, that's some fine pie." Save the file (you don't have to close it).

In the SMAPI window, enter this:

[code]patch reload UniqueID[/code]
Replace UniqueID with your UniqueID, you know, the YourUsernameHere.YourModNameHere thing. No need for the _ModdersPie part, only include the UniqueID itself.

For example, I would enter:

[code]patch reload SiTheGreat1.ModdersPie[/code]
Now take a look at that pie in-game again.

[img]https://staticdelivery.nexusmods.com/mods/1303/images/43811/43811-1773814484-1021479210.png[/img]

You'll see the description has changed! Patch reload is another Content Patcher command, which allows you to keep the game open while making and testing your mods. This way you don't have to keep opening and closing the game. Nifty, huh? Feel free to change the description back now, or keep it, whichever you prefer.

Welp, that's it! You have successfully made a mod! Woo!

Now comes what many experienced modders consider to be the hardest part of all:

Making the mod page.


[b][size=5]The Mod Page[/size]
[/b]
Technically speaking, there's nothing complex about the mod page. The difficulty lies in figuring out what to include and how to explain things to an audience that, more often than not, doesn't even read it before posting questions.

It's alright. We'll get through this together.

You can work on mod pages on your phone (though you'll need to upload the mod file from your computer). I'm going to assume you're using a computer for the instructions below, but a phone shouldn't be much different.

Assuming you've already made a Nexus account, find and click the Upload option along the top of the screen and click 'Upload Mod'. This will take you to the Add A Mod screen.

[b]Quick Note[/b]: Nexus released a new upload form system soon after I released this tutorial. The instructions below are geared towards the 'old/classic' system, but most of those new fields should still be the same as the old ones, just streamlined. I'll add instructions specific to the new system once I've taken some time to understand them :)

Most of the fields are fairly self-explanatory; I'll go through the more ambiguous ones:

- Select 'Items' or 'Miscellaneous' for your mod's category.

- The Current Version field should be 1.0.0
Whenever you make updates to your mod, there will be a separate area to enter version number updates. We'll see it later in the Files section.

- You can put your own username for Author, no need to put me in there :)

- Put some random gibberish in the Brief Overview and Detailed Description fields for now. You'll be able to change these before publishing, don't worry.

- Adult Content: if you have any, please be honest here. If you're not, your mod and even your account can get flagged. And I will be very disappointed in you.

- Classification: Requires Content Patcher, Requires SMAPI, and Compatible With 1.6 should all be selected. Anything else depends on if you included it. No, this mod does not work in 1.5

Once you click Save at the bottom, a blank mod page will be created for you, and you can click View Mod Page to see how it looks. It's not public yet, so others can't see it unless you grant them special access. You can find this mod page any time by clicking on your account icon and going to 'My Mods'. You can modify the mod page at any time (even after it's published) by clicking Manage in the top right.

Which means now is a great time for another 20 minute break! Use the bathroom, drink some water, and stare out a window. You've earned it.

Alright, let's continue working on the mod page by clicking Manage. We're going to save Mod Details, Media, and Documentation for last. For now, let's start with the Permissions section.

[b]Permissions
[/b]
A lot of modders use the defaults in this tab, and that's fine. But I want to make sure you're not ignoring it, because it's important to always be clear about your expectations and boundaries, and to give credit where it's due.

Look through all the options and change any of them to suit your preference. Then when you reach the Credits text box, please give SiTheGreat1 credit for creating the Modder's Pie beginner modding tutorial. I'll leave the exact wording up to you :) and I just want to make sure you get practice doing this. The Stardew modding community is built on respect and fair treatment, never forget that.

Be sure to click Save once you're done before going to the next page.

[b]Requirements and mirrors
[/b]
In the next section, you tell Nexus what mods are required to be installed so your mod can work. If you're using a framework, it needs to be here.

You don't have to include SMAPI (you can if you want to), but you do have to include Content Patcher since we used it extensively. If you're using a very recent version (2.9 s considered very recent at time of writing), mention it in the requirement notes as some players may not have updated their version yet.

If you have any other mods as dependencies, they should go here as well.

Remember to save before going to the next page.

[b]Files
[/b]
Welcome to the Files page! There's two things we need to do before uploading the Modder's Pie files.

First: look at the URL of your 'manage files' page. It should look something like this:

https://www.nexusmods.com/stardewvalley/mods/edit/?step=files&id=43811

Or like this if you're currently viewing the mod page itself:

https://www.nexusmods.com/stardewvalley/mods/43811

That number '43811' (the number WILL be different for you) is your mod's Nexus update key. Sound familiar?

That's right! It's the unfinished line in your manifest.json file! Open the file and find this line:

[code]"UpdateKeys": [ "Nexus:" ],[/code]
You're going to put that number right after 'Nexus:' in that line. Remember, your number is different from mine!

For my mod, that line now looks like this:

[code]"UpdateKeys": [ "Nexus:43811" ],[/code]
One more time, just to be sure: [b]YOUR NUMBER WILL BE DIFFERENT[/b]!

SMAPI uses that number to check your mod page for updates whenever a player opens modded Stardew. That's why you sometimes see purple text in the SMAPI window - because it sees that the mod page has a different version of the mod than the one the player has installed.

You won't need to change this number again after publishing your mod. When you create a new mod, that mod will have a different number for its mod page too.

Once your manifest.json is updated, save and close it. Now you're going to zip your mod files up.

Remember when we talked about how games 'pack' their files to reduce file size? That's what you're about to do. Right click on your mod's folder and click Send To > Compressed (Zipped) Folder. This may look a bit different on Mac and Linux, but the goal is the same - to create a zipped copy of the folder, which is what you'll be uploading to Nexus.

[img]https://staticdelivery.nexusmods.com/mods/1303/images/43811/43811-1773814511-738692863.png[/img]

Back to the Files page.

In the File version, write 1.0.0, and select 'This is the latest version of the mod' right below it. Whenever you update your mod (and therefore your version number), this is where you write the updated version number, with the 'latest version' option selected. This automatically updates your mod's version in Nexus. [b]This version number should always match the version number in your manifest.json file[/b], so if you're updating your mod, remember to update that too.

You may have seen the issue where SMAPI tells you a mod update is available, but the mod page says you already have the latest version downloaded. This happens when the modmaker accidentally forgets to update the version number in the manifest, leading to bug reports from players worried it'll affect their saves. It won't, but better to stay ahead of the problem.

In the file description, for the first release you can leave it blank or say it's the first release. Whenever you update however, you should put a quick summary of changes in here.

The File Options are your choice. Personally, I leave the first two unchecked and only check the third if there's a non-Content Patcher requirement because it's so common.

Finally, drag your zipped mod file into the 'upload file' box, and click 'Save Your File'. You mod file is now being uploaded to the servers and checked for bugs by Nexus.

NOTE: sometimes files take a while to be verified, especially if it's your first one. I recommend waiting to publish till after it's verified, because players won't be able to download it until it is. If the mod is rejected by Nexus, reach out to Nexus admin asking about it so they can have a human verify it rather than a bot. Don't worry, it happens all the time and they don't bite.

We're not going to bother with any articles unless you have a burning desire to write one. They're useful for adding info to your mod that's too long for the main mod page.

Speaking of: keep your mod page brief. It shouldn't be even a quarter as long as this tutorial page is. The shorter the better. Players will get bored and leave otherwise.

Alright, let's go to Documentation.

[b]Documentation[/b]

The important thing on this page is the changelog. For your first release, just putting one line with 'first release' is good enough. For any future updates however, you'll want to add detailed points about what you changed here. Some mod authors prefer to make a readme file or host their changelogs elsewhere. That's fine, but whatever method you choose, make sure your players can access it easily.

[b]Media[/b]

Every mod should have some images. At minimum, you need a banner image and a primary image to use for the mod icon. This tutorial mod page has a bunch of images because that's how I can add them to the mod page description to help you learn.

Feel free to get creative! But if you don't have any ideas (or you just really want this mod page thing done already), my go-to is usually a screenshot of my farmer holding the item as the banner, and the item itself as the mod icon. I've done these things for this tutorial mod page so you can see what they look like.

[b]Mod Details
[/b]
And finally, the mod page description! This has two parts.

First is the brief summary, something like 'My first mod! Adds a pie to the game.' Keep it short and sweet.

The second part, the detailed description, is what gets most people. In your case it's pretty straight forward, but it'll get harder for the first mod you make on your own :)

For now, something like this will suffice:

'Hello, this is my first mod, made following Si's tutorial 'Modder's Pie'. It adds a pie item to the game, with a recipe that you can buy from Gus after your first house upgrade. Have fun!'

Honestly you can put whatever you like here. But if you're at a loss, feel free to use the example.

[b]Publishing Your Mod
[/b]
Aaaaaaaand... That's it! You're done! Congratulations, woo-hoo!

It's entirely up to you whether you want to publish your Modder's Pie mod or not. Doing so can be great for feedback and gaining confidence, but if you'd prefer your first mod to be something cooler, I totally understand.

If you do decide to publish it, simply go to Manage > Publish Mod and click 'I'm Ready'. And add a comment to this tutorial page so I can see it and be happy. After that, go tell all your friends about your mod. Your family. Your neighbor's dog. They'll all be super proud of you, even if they have no idea what you're talking about.

If you don't, or you don't want to tell anyone, that's ok. Just promise me you'll be proud of yourself. I'll be proud of you too :) mod making is hard and you did something great.

Either way, once you're done, take a break, get more water, go to the bathroom, and do more than stare out the window this time. Go for a nice walk and do something fun. You've earned it.

[b]Resources[/b]

Last thing, I promise. Here's links to the resources above. Happy modding!
